loop.name: source-typed-operation-authorization
loop.what: New input is not admitted as text but as a typed envelope. `Principal` is exactly Human | Agent | Runtime and `Operation` is exactly Queue | Steer | Interject | InterruptAndSend (xai-message-delivery-core/src/envelope.rs:4-16). A `DeliveryEnvelope<Source, Grant, Content, Identity>` carries the principal as a private field plus a `PhantomData<Source>` marker, so `from_human` can only mint a `HumanSource` envelope and `from_agent` only an `AgentSource` one (envelope.rs:35-78). Authorization is a separate, explicit step: `OperationSet` is a bitmask whose only two named values are `QUEUE = 1<<0` and `QUEUE_AND_STEER = (1<<0)|(1<<1)` (envelope.rs:86-102), and `authorize_operation(allowed, requested)` is the single gate. The shell wires it as: humans get `OperationSet::QUEUE`, agents get `OperationSet::QUEUE_AND_STEER` (xai-grok-shell/src/session/message_delivery.rs:138, :171).
invariants: A human principal may only Queue - the shell passes OperationSet::QUEUE for HumanSource, so Steer is not reachable from a human envelope even though Operation::Steer exists.
The principal is stored, not derived at the call site: callers must use into_parts() and cannot re-label an envelope, because `source` is PhantomData and `principal` is private.
OperationSet has exactly two named constants today; Interject and InterruptAndSend are defined in `Operation` but no code path constructs a set containing them.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-closed - authorize_operation returns Err(UnsupportedOperation) and the shell maps that to HumanDeliveryError::Unsupported / ActiveMessageAdmission::Unsupported, refusing the input rather than downgrading it to a weaker operation.

loop.name: delivery-envelope-identity-triple-check
loop.what: Admission of an agent-originated message re-derives and compares three independent facts before the command is queued. The shell recomputes the expected prompt id as the literal `format!("parent-message-{}", message.message_id)` and rejects unless all three hold: `content == message.text`, `message_id == message.message_id`, and `prompt_id == parent-message-{message_id}` (xai-grok-shell/src/session/message_delivery.rs:163-169). Identity itself is a two-field pair `DeliveryIdentity<MessageId, PromptId>` whose constructor is the only way to build it (envelope.rs:22-33); for the human path the two ids are additionally required to be equal, and the grant's target session must match the handle's (message_delivery.rs:135-137). The grant type is the other half of the check: `ResidentHumanGrant{target_session_id}` and `OwnedActiveDescendantGrant{target_session_id, delivery}` are distinct structs, so a caller cannot present an agent grant on a human send path.
invariants: The prompt-id string `parent-message-{message_id}` is load-bearing and duplicated between the producer and the check; changing the producer format without the check rejects every parent message.
A grant is scoped to exactly one target_session_id; there is no wildcard or inherited grant.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-closed - any mismatch returns Rejected (human path) or ActiveMessageAdmission::Rejected (agent path) before the mpsc send.

loop.name: turn-bound-safe-point-delivery
loop.what: A message that must reach a running turn waits for a safe point instead of cutting in. `MessageDeliveryLifecycle` holds a `VecDeque<DeliverySlot>` where each slot is exactly Pending -> Projecting -> Delivered and each slot carries a `TurnBinding<PromptId, Epoch>` (xai-message-delivery-core/src/lifecycle.rs:74-78, :115-117). The three-phase protocol is explicit: `begin_delivery` moves this turn's Pending slots to Projecting and returns their messages, then `finish_delivery` runs a caller-supplied `commit` closure and only promotes Projecting to Delivered if the commit returns Ok (lifecycle.rs:195-254). A failed commit therefore leaves the messages Projecting, i.e. still unsettled, rather than lost. `transition(TerminalTarget::Turn | All, TerminalCause)` settles everything at end of turn, and the cause decides the disposition - `Completion | SoftCancel | Rewind` fall back (re-queue), while `HardTeardown | ActorDrop` complete as errors (lifecycle.rs:90-103, :256-287). The shell additionally caps live steer slots with `MAX_PARENT_STEER_SLOTS = 32` so one batch of parent text stays finite, and a `Drop` impl settles all slots with a terminal error if the owner disappears (xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/parent_message.rs:45-47, :83-97).
invariants: Delivery is not delivery until the commit closure succeeds: Projecting is the only state from which a commit can promote.
A `TurnBinding` is (prompt_id, epoch), not just prompt_id - a rewind that reuses a prompt id but bumps the epoch does not match the old slots.
The lifecycle is append-unique by identity: `admit_pending` returns the message back as Err if that identity is already present in any slot.
ActorDrop must settle every slot: leaving a slot Pending would strand a caller awaiting its oneshot.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-closed - an uncommitted batch stays Projecting (neither delivered nor dropped) and terminal settlement routes it either to fallbacks (re-queue) or to an explicit error completion; nothing is silently discarded.

loop.name: mid-turn-interjection-framing
loop.what: Input that arrives while a turn runs is buffered, then drained as synthetic user messages rather than injected as a system note. `InterjectionBuffer<Attachment>` is a type alias for `EventQueue<PendingInterjection<Attachment>>` (xai-interjection-core/src/buffer.rs:24), and `drain_formatted` drains all pending entries and frames each one separately - FIFO, one message per entry, explicitly never merged (buffer.rs:26-42). Framing is a fixed three-part envelope built by `frame_user_turn`: a leading note, the message wrapped by `user_query` in `<user_query>...</user_query>`, and a trailing `UNFINISHED_TASKS_REMINDER` that reads `Make sure to complete any unfinished tasks from previous turns.` (format.rs:8-24). Two notes exist for two situations - `INTERJECTION_NOTE = "The user sent a message while you were working:"` for a mid-turn steer and `INTERRUPT_NOTE = "The user interrupted the previous turn:"` for the next real query after a text-only mid-turn abort (format.rs:4-5, :43-51). Text longer than `LARGE_PROMPT_THRESHOLD = 25_000` bytes is truncated at a UTF-8 character boundary and suffixed `... [truncated]` (format.rs:1-2, :26-39).
invariants: The trailing unfinished-tasks reminder is part of the contract, not decoration: every interjection and interrupt carries it, and a test pins that it follows the closing `</user_query>` tag.
One message per buffered entry - `drain_formatted` never merges, which is the opposite of the queued-prompt combine rule in xai-prompt-queue.
Truncation must land on a char boundary; the implementation walks char_indices rather than slicing at the byte offset.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-soft - oversize text is truncated with a visible marker rather than rejected; an empty buffer drains to an empty vec, and sanitization is a caller-supplied function whose absence is spelled as `std::convert::identity`.

constants.name: INTERJECTION_NOTE
constants.value: "The user sent a message while you were working:"

loop.name: queued-prompt-combine-with-versioned-edit
loop.what: Follow-up prompts queued behind a running turn can be merged into one turn under a pure, shared eligibility rule. `combine_prefix_len` walks the queue from the front and returns the mergeable prefix length: the front must be a plain prompt (`can_merge_front` - not synthetic, not an expanded skill, not bash, non-empty text, images allowed) and each follower must additionally carry no images and not be under edit hold (`can_merge_follower`) (xai-prompt-queue/src/combine.rs:29-60). Merged bodies are joined with a blank-line separator `TEXT_SEPARATOR = "\n\n"` (combine.rs:9, :62-68) and, when two or more originals merged, the per-prompt display texts are stamped into content-block `_meta` under `COMBINED_DISPLAY_TEXTS_META = "combinedDisplayTexts"` so the UI can rebuild multi-bubble display from one model turn (types.rs:3-5, combine.rs:70-93). Queue rows are edited in place under optimistic concurrency: `QueueEntryMeta.version` is a monotonic counter bumped on every edit and `owner` is explicitly never overwritten by edits, only `last_editor` is (types.rs:10-26). The whole queue is mirrored to clients as one `QueueChanged` broadcast keyed by `sessionId`, carrying `entries` plus a separately-reported `running_prompt_id`/`running_text` because the running row is deliberately omitted from `entries` (types.rs:53-76).
invariants: Eligibility for merging lives in one pure module shared by the pager's local drain and the shell's promote path, so the stop conditions cannot drift between them.
The running row is never present in `entries`; a client must read `runningPromptId`/`runningText` or it will show a queue with a hole.
`owner` is immutable under edit - only `last_editor` moves.
A `QueueChanged` without `sessionId` must fail to parse rather than apply under the wrong key.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-soft - an ineligible front yields prefix length 1 (take the front alone), so combining simply does not happen; an unknown extra field deserializes and is ignored for forward compatibility.

loop.name: canonical-turn-event-log
loop.what: Each session writes an append-only `events.jsonl` whose rows are a pinned, tagged event taxonomy rather than free-form logging. `EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION = "1.0"` is stamped on the turn-scoped rows (xai-grok-session-events/src/types.rs:3, :15), and `Event` is a `#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]` enum covering the loop's observable states: TurnStarted (with turn_number, model_id, yolo_mode, conversation_message_count, session_relationship), PhaseChanged, FirstToken, LoopStarted{loop_index}, ToolStarted, ToolCompleted (duration_ms, outcome, source, rewriting_hook), PermissionRequested, PermissionResolved (decision, wait_ms), TurnEnded (outcome, cancellation_category, cancellation_context), Interjected (source, image_count, redirect_kind) and YoloToggled (types.rs:5-62). The `EventTracker` holds the mutable per-turn counters the events are derived from - active tool, tool count this turn, and one-shot `prior_interrupt_category` / `prior_redirect_kind` markers that survive `begin_turn` (tracker.rs:84-183).
invariants: `schema_version` is a field on the turn-scoped rows, so a reader can branch per row rather than per file.
The prior-interrupt and prior-redirect markers are one-shot `take_*` values that deliberately survive begin_turn; they describe the previous turn, and a test pins that.
Wire labels are pinned by test: tool outcomes, cancellation categories, redirect kinds and interjection tags must round-trip.
loop.failurePolicy: fail-soft - the writer holds `Mutex<Option<File>>` and swallows open and write failures after logging once behind an AtomicBool error_logged latch; `EventWriter::noop()` exists so an unwritable session still runs (log.rs:28-81).

session.name: filesystem-probed-journal-mode-with-per-host-db
session.what: This crate is not an event log - it contains no append API, no event rows and no crash repair. It is a filesystem-aware `PRAGMA journal_mode` selector plus a per-host database path derivation. `JournalMode::for_db_path` classifies the database's parent directory through `is_network_fs` and returns `Wal` on a local filesystem or `Truncate` on a network one (xai-sqlite-journal/src/lib.rs:43-82); `Truncate.effective_db_path` then rewrites the filename to a per-host sibling (`worktrees.db` -> `worktrees.h-<host>.db`) using a lowercased-alphanumeric hostname discriminator capped at 24 characters (lib.rs:108-133). `apply` orders `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` -> `journal_mode=TRUNCATE` -> `locking_mode=NORMAL` so converting an already-WAL-stamped database never mmaps a `-shm` file (lib.rs:199-209). The module doc gives the concrete failure being avoided: WAL keeps its wal-index in an mmap'd `-shm`, and when `$HOME` is NFS-mounted a peer host truncating or rebuilding that file during recovery rips the mapping out and the next wal-index read dies with SIGBUS (lib.rs:1-13). The read-only open on the Truncate arm deliberately opens READ_WRITE without CREATE and then sets `query_only=true`, because POSIX forbids write-locking an O_RDONLY file descriptor (lib.rs:151-183). The network magic list covers NFS/SMB/SMB2/CIFS/9p/CODA/AFS/kAFS/CEPH/Lustre/GFS2/GPFS/OCFS2/WekaFS/FUSE (lib.rs:353-376); on macOS the authoritative signal is the absence of `MNT_LOCAL` (lib.rs:401-411); on Windows it probes UNC prefixes and `GetDriveTypeW == DRIVE_REMOTE` (lib.rs:478-513). Five consumers are wired: xai-fast-worktree, xai-grok-dashboard-store, xai-grok-foreign-sessions, xai-grok-memory and xai-grok-session-search.
invariants: Callers must create the parent directory before calling `for_db_path`, because classification reads the directory and the DB file may not exist yet.
Per-host suffixing must stay idempotent, or a sidecar file operation would re-suffix an already-resolved path.
WAL must never be selected for a database on a network filesystem; the per-host path is what makes that hold even against an old binary that stamps WAL.
Converting a WAL-stamped DB to TRUNCATE must go through EXCLUSIVE locking before the journal_mode change and back to NORMAL after.
`apply` must set `busy_timeout` first or go through `apply_with_retry`, because lock paths only partially honor the busy handler.
session.failurePolicy: mixed - detection fails OPEN to WAL (`is_network_fs` returns false on any statfs error), the env kill-switch fails loud-but-open (an invalid value warns and falls through to detection), and mode application fails CLOSED after a bounded retry whose error is re-wrapped with the elapsed time.

constants.name: RETRY_PAUSE
constants.value: 20 ms, with a per-attempt busy clamp of 20 ms..1000 ms

session.name: pid-liveness-active-session-registry-with-atomic-replace
session.what: Open sessions are tracked in `~/.grok/active_sessions.json` so an unclean exit is detectable rather than invisible, and every mutation is a locked read-modify-write. `with_locked_state` takes a blocking exclusive `fs2` lock on `active_sessions.lock`, reads the JSON array, applies a closure, then atomically replaces the file via write-temp plus `fs::rename`, cleaning the temp file up if the rename fails (xai-grok-active-sessions/src/lib.rs:81-130). A separate `try_with_locked_state` uses `try_lock_exclusive` so a signal handler never blocks (lib.rs:141-158). `collect_crashed_in` partitions entries on `is_pid_alive` and returns only the dead ones (lib.rs:173-204); on unix an EPERM probe counts as alive (lib.rs:184).
invariants: Every write must go through the tempfile-plus-rename path, or a crash mid-write truncates the registry.
A `try_unregister` that returns false on contention must leave the entry intact for next-launch reaping - it does, because the closure never runs.
The blocking and non-blocking variants must share one `locked_mutate`, so their semantics cannot drift apart.
PID-liveness is the only liveness signal, so a recycled PID can make a crashed session look live; the design accepts this and reports only dead-PID orphans.
session.failurePolicy: mixed - the registry read is fail-open (a missing file, an empty file, or corrupt JSON all yield an empty list, with a warning only for corruption), IO errors other than NotFound propagate, lock contention in the non-blocking path is a soft `Ok(false)`/`Ok(None)`, and PID probing degrades to 'assume alive' on unsupported platforms.
session.wiringNote: Wired, but thin: `collect_crashed()` runs at process start (xai-grok-pager-bin/src/main.rs:1973) and only logs the count. The returned Vec<ActiveSession> has no consumer beyond that log line.

session.name: epoch-versioned-single-flight-gateway-catalog
session.what: A gateway tool catalog is fetched behind a single-flight gate that cannot resurrect a disabled catalog. `ManagedMcpState` keeps a `gateway_tool_epoch` that is bumped by `enable`/`disable`, and `complete_gateway_tool_fetch(epoch, ..)` commits the fetched catalog only if the epoch still matches, so a fetch that was in flight when the catalog was disabled is discarded rather than applied (xai-grok-shell-session-support/src/managed_mcp.rs:43-87, :304-355). `get_or_fetch_gateway_tool_catalog` single-flights waiters on a `tokio::sync::Notify` and rolls the state back to `NotFetched` on failure, so a later caller retries instead of inheriting a poisoned result. An `Err` is deliberately distinct from `Ok(empty_catalog)` - a failed fetch and an genuinely empty catalog are different states (managed_mcp.rs:131).
invariants: A completed fetch must be epoch-checked before commit; without it a stale in-flight response silently re-enables a disabled catalog.
The epoch is bumped on both enable and disable, so the check does not assume the direction of the change.
Failure must roll back to `NotFetched` rather than caching the error, or one transient failure would permanently deny the catalog.
`Err` and `Ok(empty)` must stay distinguishable at the API boundary.
session.failurePolicy: fail-soft with an explicit distinction - a failed fetch does not populate the cache and does not read as an empty catalog; waiters are released through a Notify rather than polling.

session.name: dashboard-capacity-eviction-with-schema-gate
session.what: The dashboard workspace store enforces a hard capacity inside one immediate transaction and refuses rather than silently dropping pinned rows. `insert_member_inner` runs a single IMMEDIATE transaction that, at capacity, evicts `count - (capacity - 1)` least-recently-changed UNPINNED rows ordered by `last_change_unix_ms, session_id, kind`; if no row is unpinned it returns `StoreError::AllPinned` having written nothing (xai-grok-dashboard-store/src/store.rs:212-248). A newer on-disk `PRAGMA user_version` short-circuits to `open_newer_schema` with `PRAGMA query_only=true`, so an older binary reads a newer store read-only instead of corrupting it (store_open.rs:97). The store states an ownership contract in its own doc: it owns every byte of that SQL, consumers get only the typed API, and every statement names its columns so decode indexes never depend on table order (xai-grok-dashboard-store/src/lib.rs:1-14).
invariants: Eviction and insert must be one transaction, or a failed insert can leave rows evicted.
Pinned rows are never evicted; if only pinned rows remain the operation fails with `AllPinned` and writes nothing rather than exceeding capacity.
A newer schema must be opened read-only through `query_only`, never migrated downward.
Columns are named explicitly in every statement so additive schema evolution cannot clobber a column an older binary does not know about.
session.failurePolicy: fail-closed on capacity (refuse with `AllPinned` rather than violate the bound) and fail-safe on schema version (read-only open instead of a downgrade).
session.wiringNote: The entire store is host-gated OFF BY DEFAULT behind `GROK_WORKSPACE_DASHBOARD` (xai-grok-pager/src/app/event_loop.rs:1257). `remove_member`, `set_pin_rank`, `rekey` and `data_version()` have no shipped callers - tests only.

session.name: append-only-jsonl-session-event-log
session.what: Each session writes an append-only `events.jsonl` of typed events, and in this tree nothing reads it back. `EventWriter::open` uses `create(true).append(true)` and, on an open failure, warns once and stores a `None` file slot so a writer is always constructible; clones share one `Arc<EventWriterInner>` holding `Mutex<Option<File>>`, making the writer `Clone + Send + Sync` for background tasks (xai-grok-session-events/src/log.rs:34-51). Each line is an RFC3339 millisecond UTC timestamp flattened with the internally-tagged `Event` (log.rs:62-81).
invariants: `emit` must never panic and must not propagate: it returns unit and drops the line on a serialization or lock failure.
The write-error warning stays behind an `error_logged` swap so a broken disk cannot log once per event.
`EventWriter::noop()` must be indistinguishable from a working writer to callers - it pre-sets the latch so it never warns.
session.failurePolicy: fail-open and silent by design - an open failure, a poisoned mutex and a serialization failure all return without emitting.
session.wiringNote: Wired for the local TUI - `EventTracker::new` is called with no env gate at xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/spawn.rs:1864. The WORKSPACE host is gated off by default: `get_or_open_session_writer(enabled=false)` returns a noop writer and creates no directory (xai-grok-workspace/src/session/mod.rs:1026-1028), where enabled is `GROK_WORKSPACE_EVENTS_ENABLED == "true"` (xai-grok-workspace/src/handle.rs:4585). A repo-wide search for `events.jsonl` finds writers and tests only - no non-test reader exists in this tree. Treat the 'write-only' characterisation as grep-derived: a reader that builds the filename dynamically would not have been caught.

session.name: bounded-metadata-only-foreign-session-scan
session.what: Other coding agents' session stores are read as metadata with hard caps, not ingested. The module doc describes the shape as a bounded, metadata-only listing (xai-grok-foreign-sessions/src/lib.rs:1-6), and the bounds are declared constants: at most 50 sessions per tool, a maximum session age of 30 days, a 200-character title cap, and a 5-minute tolerance for timestamps that appear to come from the future (lib.rs:20-23). The public surface is narrow - a full scan and a `most_recent_foreign_session` convenience - so the caller gets a listing and not a parser for foreign formats.
invariants: Metadata only: the caps make it structurally impossible for a foreign store to pull unbounded content into this process.
MAX_FUTURE_SKEW exists because a clock skew between agents must not let a session be treated as recent indefinitely.
The title is truncated, so a hostile or pathological foreign title cannot blow up display or index sizes.
session.failurePolicy: fail-soft - bounded listing degrades to fewer rows; a foreign store that cannot be read contributes nothing rather than failing the caller.

context.name: single-source-token-estimation
context.what: Token accounting is one shared, deliberately crude heuristic rather than per-consumer arithmetic. The crate doc states the intent plainly: it is the single source of truth for the bytes/4 heuristic and the derived-display arithmetic used by `/context`, `/session-info`, the auto-compact gates, the preflight overflow check, and every client renderer (xai-token-estimation/src/lib.rs:1-6). The primitives are `estimate_tokens`/`estimate_chars` over `BYTES_PER_TOKEN = 4` and a separate flat `IMAGE_TOKEN_ESTIMATE = 765` applied per image by `estimate_image_tokens` (lib.rs:9, :13, :17-31). Threshold decisions are also centralized: `exceeds_threshold` and `exceeds_threshold_with_headroom` are the only predicates, and percentage display is split into three variants (`usage_percentage`, `usage_percentage_u8`, `usage_percentage_truncated_u8`) so a renderer picks a rounding behaviour instead of inventing one (lib.rs:38-89).
invariants: Every consumer that talks about context-window usage must route through this crate; the crate doc explicitly enumerates the five consumers so a new one is a visible addition.
Images are estimated by a flat per-image constant, not by decoding dimensions - the estimate is deliberately not content-aware.
An overflow check and the number shown to the user must use the same predicate, which is why the threshold helpers live here rather than at each call site.
context.failurePolicy: fail-soft - the estimate is a heuristic that under- or over-counts; the fail-safe direction is supplied by the headroom variant rather than by the estimator, which has no error path at all (the functions are total).

context.name: compaction-transcript-rendering-with-byte-caps
context.what: A compacted segment is rendered into self-contained markdown by a pure, I/O-free function rather than being summarized into an opaque blob. The crate doc describes it as pure rendering of a compacted segment into self-contained markdown aligned with a Python reference implementation (`render_segment_to_markdown` / `compute_turn_stats`, with an index built incrementally through `INDEX_HEADER` + `render_index_row`), matching headers, sections, detail levels and INDEX columns but not bytes (xai-compaction-transcript/src/lib.rs:1-6). Segments are written as `segment_<n>` files under a `compaction` directory with an `INDEX.md`, and each segment is bounded at `SEGMENT_MAX_BYTES = 512 * 1024` with a recorded truncation notice (lib.rs:16-22). Detail levels are expressed as character budgets - `BALANCED_TEXT_CHARS = 2000`, `BALANCED_RESPONSE_CHARS = 500`, `LAST_RESPONSE_EXCERPT_CHARS = 500` - plus a flat `PER_TURN_OVERHEAD_BYTES = 64` (lib.rs:25-30).
invariants: The renderer is pure and performs no I/O; the caller owns writing, which is what makes the output reproducible.
Segment size is capped at 512 KiB, so a single pathological turn cannot produce an unbounded segment file.
Truncation is recorded in the output via a notice constant rather than being silent - a reader can tell a truncated segment from a complete one.
Format alignment with the Python implementation is a stated goal at the section/detail/column level; byte-identity is explicitly not.
context.failurePolicy: fail-soft - over-budget content is truncated with a notice; the crate has no failure path because it performs no I/O.

context.name: full-replace-compaction-rather-than-tail-retention
context.what: grok's compaction is a FULL REPLACE: it summarises the whole conversation and rebuilds a fresh history rather than keeping a recent tail, so there is no tail-budget or split-point policy on the shipped path. `sample_summary_with_retries` calls the compaction sampler up to `max_attempts` times, accepting a non-empty summary whose cleaned seed passes `is_degenerate_summary`, treating empty or degenerate output as transient, and short-circuiting deterministic failures (xai-grok-compaction/src/code_compaction/compact.rs:53-73, :87-98). Failures are returned structurally as a typed error carrying `message`, `deterministic` and `context_overflow` so the host can choose between suppressing auto-compaction and stepping its own input ladder. The lossy summary is then made recoverable by a pointer, not by retained turns: `CompactionMode` is Summary (no pointer), Transcript (pointer to the raw `updates.jsonl`) or Segments(CompactionDetail), and `transcript_hint` returns None if the mode adds no pointer OR no location is available, so the model is never pointed at nothing (xai-chat-state/src/compaction_mode.rs:12-25, :49-83). `CompactionDetail` is a separate four-level axis (None/Minimal/Balanced/Verbose, default Verbose) that attaches only to Segments.
invariants: A context-length overflow must be reported with BOTH `context_overflow` and `deterministic` set, because re-sending the same payload is guaranteed to fail again - retrying it is pure waste.
`CompactionMode::default()` must stay `Segments(CompactionDetail::default())`, i.e. Verbose; this is the shipped default and a change silently reduces recoverable detail.
Detail must attach only to `Segments` - the other modes ignore it, so attaching it elsewhere would expose a meaningless setting.
The retry loop must stay content-neutral: the harness builds the prompt and cleans the winning summary, so the loop cannot bias content.
context.failurePolicy: fail-closed to the caller - a typed terminal error and no partially applied compaction; individual transient attempts are retried after a delay.

constants.name: MIN_SUMMARY_SEED_CHARS
constants.value: 500 (doc note: smallest healthy prod summary observed was ~3,242 chars)

context.wiringNote: Mostly INERT in this tree. The crate is a real engine (36 src files, no cargo features) and the shell does call `sample_full_replace_summary` (xai-grok-shell/src/session/compaction.rs:1138), but `apply_intra_compaction`, `should_compact`, `inter_compaction`, `history::filter`/`history::validate`, `select.rs`, `fit.rs`, `assemble_compacted_history`, `apply_full_replace_compaction`, `wrap_user_query` and `validate_compaction_text` have callers only inside the crate's own tests - the shell uses xai-chat-state's duplicated `compaction_utils` copies instead. `IntraCompactionConfig::default()` sets `enabled: false` (crates/common/xai-grok-compaction/src/intra_compaction/config.rs:227). The tool-pair-safe split selector in particular is UNWIRED: `select_turns_to_compact` walks backward accumulating keep-tokens and `snap_to_safe_boundary` advances past a contiguous run of tool results so a split can never orphan a tool result, returning None rather than 'compact everything' when nothing should move (crates/common/xai-grok-compaction/src/select.rs:60-147) - but its only callers are intra_compaction/compact.rs:505 and fit.rs:148, in the unwired chain.

context.name: boundary-exact-token-gate-and-image-budget-hysteresis
context.what: Two distinct budget mechanisms with deliberately different shapes. (a) The token gate is boundary-exact integer arithmetic: `exceeds_threshold` computes `used*100 >= window*threshold` so it fires exactly AT the threshold, which is one token earlier than a legacy `>` gate, and `exceeds_threshold_with_headroom` is the same scaled comparison minus `headroom*100` (xai-token-estimation/src/lib.rs:78-102). The display helpers deliberately differ from each other - `usage_percentage_u8` ROUNDS while `usage_percentage_truncated_u8` TRUNCATES - because a test pins that `exceeds_threshold(used, window, p)` agrees with `truncated(used, window) >= p` (lib.rs:48-64). (b) Image eviction is a hysteresis loop rather than a threshold: `apply_image_budget` measures the exact serialized conversation body and evicts inline images oldest-first only when the body reaches a high-water trigger, reclaiming down to a strictly lower low-water mark (xai-chat-state/src/image_budget.rs:20-60). Measurement is exact but allocation-free: `conversation_body_bytes` blanks every image URL, serializes through a byte-counting `io::Write` sink, then adds back each URL's exact escaped contribution (image_budget.rs:244-321).
invariants: `exceeds_threshold` must keep `>=` semantics and the `context_window == 0 -> false` short-circuit, or callers would have to special-case a missing window.
`usage_percentage_truncated_u8` must keep truncating while `usage_percentage_u8` rounds; collapsing them breaks the agreement test between the gate and the displayed number.
All products in the gate must stay saturating so a huge window cannot wrap.
The image reclaim target must stay strictly BELOW the trigger - this is enforced by a compile-time assert, because otherwise every turn at the ceiling re-evicts and re-busts the prompt cache.
Below the trigger the request history must stay byte-identical so the KV prefix remains stable.
context.failurePolicy: mixed. The token gate is pure and total (zero window returns false, overflow saturates, no error path). The image budget fails soft in the under-measuring direction: if serialization fails the byte counter keeps what it counted so far - a lower bound - and warns, so a measurement bug cannot force a needless eviction.
context.wiringNote: Both wired on every request build; the image budget emits a `ChatStateEvent::ImageBudget` for observability. Note a real boundary asymmetry rather than a defect: this helper fires at `used == threshold`, while the intra-compaction trigger uses strict `>` (crates/common/xai-grok-compaction/src/intra_compaction/trigger.rs:143).

context.name: structured-context-length-error-classifier
context.what: Because backends report a size overflow with no stable error code, one shared predicate defines it. `is_context_length_error` is used by the turn path, the harness compaction classifiers and the shared retry loop, and it matches three classes: unanchored prose ("too long for this model", "prompt is too long", "maximum prompt length", "maximum context length", "maximum allowed number of bytes", and the pair "current message" + "exceeds budget"); ANCHORED provider slugs (`context_length_exceeded`, `exceed_context_size_error`, `payload_too_large`, each required at message start or immediately after `": "`); and rendered 413 reason phrases in legacy, RFC-9110 and RFC-2616 spellings (xai-grok-compaction/src/code_compaction/failure.rs:9-58).
invariants: The anchored variants must stay anchored: the test table explicitly pins that echoed prose, an echoed slug, and a stray digit run next to a phrase must NOT classify.
`input length` and `exceeds the maximum allowed length` must be required as a PAIR, so field-length validation errors do not classify as size overflows.
Because the predicate is deterministic, callers must not retry on a match - a match means the same payload will fail again.
context.failurePolicy: fail-open in the safe direction - an unmatched message is treated as transient and retried, while a false positive is deterministic and suppresses retry. Pure function, no IO, no error path.

context.name: project-instruction-injection-into-user-message
context.what: Project instruction files (AGENTS.md, Claude.md, vendor rules directories) are read from `~/.grok/`, the git repository root and the session cwd, deduped by canonical path with a project-over-rule preference, then rendered by `render_agents_md` into a single `<system-reminder>` block ordered repo-root then cwd, with a note that deeper files take precedence on conflicts (xai-grok-agent/src/prompt/agents_md.rs:140, :300-332). The block is delivered in the USER MESSAGE rather than the system prompt, and rule files are reduced to their body via `extract_skill_body` before rendering. The leading bytes of the block are a compatibility contract: `LEGACY_AGENTS_MD_REMINDER_PREFIX` is what the shell matches to detect an untagged legacy copy on a resumed session, so changing it breaks resume de-duplication (agents_md.rs:306).
invariants: Untrusted file content must be neutralized before interpolation: `neutralize_reminder_tags` HTML-escapes a leading `<` on `<system-reminder>`/`<system_reminder>`, so a repository's AGENTS.md cannot break out of or forge harness framing.
The literal leading bytes are a wire-format contract used for legacy detection on resumed sessions.
gitignore IS honored for instruction-file discovery - but deliberately NOT for skill-root discovery, which is a different traversal with a different rule.
context.failurePolicy: fail-soft - an unreadable candidate is dropped through a `filter_map` over `read_to_string(...).ok()`, and an empty set renders to None rather than an empty reminder block.

tools.name: validate-then-freeze-tool-registry
tools.what: A toolset is not usable until a validation pass succeeds and the registry is frozen. `validate_config(&ToolServerConfig)` returns `Vec<RequirementError>` and checks, in order: the behavior preset exists, the tool id is registered, the behavior version resolves, params deserialize into the typed params struct, client-facing names are unique, and the standard (`read_file`/`search_replace`/`grep`) and hashline file-tool bundles are not mixed (xai-grok-tools/src/registry/types.rs:795-938). `finalize_with_trunc_config` re-runs that validation and returns `Err(errors)` before building the immutable finalized toolset (registry/types.rs:963-973). Out-of-tree tool packs invert the dependency via `register_tool_pack` with a documented ordering contract - registration must happen before the first `ToolRegistryBuilder::new()` (registry/types.rs:27-51).
invariants: Finalization is validate-then-freeze: there is no path that produces a mutable toolset, and any validation error prevents a toolset from existing at all.
A config `kind` that deserializes to `ToolKind::Other` must warn, because a silent `Other` demotes the tool in the restrictive subagent capability modes.
Tool packs must register before the first builder construction; the ordering is a contract, not an implementation detail.
Validation short-circuits after each stage so errors are reported one class at a time - a caller fixing one class reveals the next.
tools.failurePolicy: fail-closed - any RequirementError makes finalize return Err and no toolset is produced.

constants.name: standard file bundle
constants.value: GrokBuild:read_file | search_replace | grep; hashline bundle GrokBuildHashline:hashline_read | hashline_edit | hashline_grep

tools.name: declarative-tool-requirement-and-params-validation
tools.what: Two declarative layers guard every tool config rather than ad-hoc checks. `Expr<T>` is a generic boolean tree - `Value`, `And`, `Or`, `Not`, `True`, `False` - evaluated by a caller-supplied closure, with `ToolRequirement` variants `Tool`, `ToolKind`, `IfParams` and `InputParam` (xai-grok-tools/src/types/requirements.rs:17-59, :110-198). The whole tree is evaluated in one loop against the resolved toolset (registry/types.rs:928-936). `InputParam` is the sharp one: it verifies the referenced parameter is actually visible in the dependent tool's JSON schema, which is needed because description templates interpolate `${{ params.<kind>.<param> }}` and a reference to a non-existent param would render as text rather than fail (requirements.rs:134-139, :187-195). Parameter validation separately deserializes through `serde_path_to_error` to obtain the failing field path, classifies the serde message into a stable category, then runs the type's own `validate_params_value` for semantic checks (xai-grok-tools/src/types/params_validation.rs:44-73, categories at :119-131).
invariants: Requirements are evaluated against the proposed configuration including params, not against static metadata - `ToolKind { if_params }` requires at least one tool of that kind whose params actually satisfy the expression.
`IfParams` is vacuously true when its condition is false, so an inapplicable requirement cannot accidentally block.
A params type must implement `ResourceType` to be validatable; effective params are merged only after validation passes.
tools.failurePolicy: fail-closed - an unsatisfied requirement yields an `unsatisfied requirements` error and blocks finalization.

tools.name: bounded-tool-output-with-mcp-spill
tools.what: Tool output is bounded in bytes at several layers, and an oversized MCP payload is spilled to disk with a pointer rather than dropped. The built-in bounds are `DEFAULT_TOOL_OUTPUT_BYTES = 40_000` and `DEFAULT_TOOL_OUTPUT_CHARS = 20_000` (xai-grok-tools/src/lib.rs:7, :11), with a `TruncationConfig` resolving per-tool over default and keeping a separate `mcp_max_output_bytes` so an MCP-specific override never changes non-MCP readers (xai-grok-tools/src/types/context.rs:16-61). `truncate_mcp_text` writes the full payload into the session's `mcp/` directory and appends a pointer plus a tool-specific steering hint (xai-grok-tools/src/util/mcp_truncate.rs:200-219). Two strategies are distinguished rather than conflated: `truncate_line` discards beyond the limit while `soft_wrap_line` preserves all content for tools where the whole output matters (xai-grok-tools/src/util/truncate.rs:12-21, :47-56), and `truncate_with_preview` always states the real total size even when the text on hand fits (truncate.rs:129-158).
invariants: The spill filename is sanitized from the wire-supplied `call_id`, so a `/` or `..` cannot escape the session `mcp/` directory.
All truncation is UTF-8-boundary-safe; `truncate_str` walks back at most 3 bytes.
The MCP cap is resolved host-side once and published process-wide so free-function dispatch sees the same value as the config path.
The reported total size is the real one, not the size of the retained excerpt.
tools.failurePolicy: fail-soft - content is degraded with an explicit footer rather than silently dropped, and a missing session folder simply omits the spill file.

tools.name: concurrent-tool-dispatch-with-per-path-serialization
tools.what: A batch of tool calls is prepared sequentially - approval, hooks, argument remapping - then dispatched concurrently, and each result is committed to state as it arrives rather than after the whole batch. `execute_tool_calls` splits an `exit_plan_mode` tail out of a multi-call batch so plan approval acts as a barrier, then runs the two batches in order (xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/tool_calls.rs:384-437). `execute_tool_calls_batch` builds one future per approved call, pushes them into a `futures::stream::FuturesUnordered`, and drains them through an unbounded channel in a completion loop that takes the matching approved slot and runs post-tool-use handling per item (tool_calls.rs:935-960). Write conflicts are serialized by a per-path `tokio::sync::Mutex` map built only from calls whose `is_read_only` is false (tool_calls.rs:653-670, :815-823), and `lock_path_for_args` canonicalizes the existing ancestor so two spellings of the same file share one lock (xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/tool_dispatch.rs:53-86). A separate FIFO lock manager with writer-starvation avoidance exists beneath at `FileOperationLockManager` (xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/editor_infra/file_operation_lock.rs:1-114).
invariants: Two calls keying the same path must share a lock and therefore run in model-emitted order; returning no key is what means genuinely concurrent.
A read-only call must never enter the write-lock set.
One index maps to exactly one approved slot - the completion loop takes rather than indexes.
A permission rejection on any call must still answer every remaining call in the batch with a cancelled result so the provider's call/result pairing stays intact.
tools.failurePolicy: mixed - the stream-drain barrier before emitting calls is fail-open on timeout (proceed) but a revoked boundary aborts the turn; a permission reject fails the batch closed while still pairing every tool_result.

tools.name: backoff-ladder-plus-server-signalled-doom-loop-recovery
tools.what: There are two independent retry systems and they are deliberately not the same one. Generic exponential backoff is `BackoffConfig { max_retries, base_delay_ms, max_delay_ms }` with `calculate_delay` doubling and clamping to the cap, driven by `execute_with_backoff` which invokes an `on_retry(attempt, max, delay)` callback before sleeping (xai-grok-tools/src/retry.rs:11-95); live call sites use 5 retries / 5 s base / 60 s cap for the model catalog and 5 / 2 s / 30 s for a post-unblock JWT retry. Repeat-tool and doom-loop recovery is NOT client-detected: the server emits a non-standard `response.doom_loop_check` SSE event with a cumulative trigger set, parsed into a signal type with an `Unknown` fallback (xai-grok-sampling-types/src/doom_loop.rs:33, :169-195), governed by a recovery policy and retried under its own backoff (xai-grok-sampler/src/retry.rs:30). Turn-level transient retries are separately bounded (xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/sampler_turn.rs:19-30, :66-72).
invariants: Tool failures are explicitly not fed to the doom-loop detector - error-count streaks were removed as a signal.
`DoomLoopSignal::parse` must never fail: any grammar mismatch becomes `Unknown` with the raw label preserved, so a server-side evolution cannot break the client.
Only a confident trigger set resamples - an `Unknown` signal degrades rather than triggering recovery.
The doom-loop marker is ignored when it appears inside a text delta; it is matched as a structured event, not by substring.
tools.failurePolicy: fail-soft - an unparseable or unconfident signal degrades to no recovery; transient turn retries are bounded by both a count and a wall-clock window so retries cannot continue indefinitely.

tools.name: lazy-tool-exposure-via-search-index
tools.what: Not every available tool is exposed to the model at once. A `ToolSearchIndex` trait is defined in the tools crate precisely to stay backend-agnostic, implemented in the shell, and returns a `SearchSnapshot { results, total_hidden_tools, is_ready }`; a `ToolIndex` wraps it as an injected resource (xai-grok-tools/src/types/tool_index.rs:29-74). The model reaches hidden tools through `search_tool` / `use_tool` meta-tools. The readiness flag is part of the contract rather than an internal detail: `is_ready = false` means the index is still warming and results may be incomplete, which consumers must distinguish from a genuine no-match (tool_index.rs:35-37).
invariants: The trait must carry no MCP-specific concepts - the concrete implementation maps its own initialization state onto `is_ready`.
`is_ready = false` must be surfaced, not collapsed into an empty result, or a cold index reads as 'this tool does not exist'.
A static index must be `Send + Sync` because it is injected as a shared resource.
tools.failurePolicy: fail-open on index warmth (partial results are returned with the flag set) and fail-closed on call time (an unavailable tool cannot be invoked).

tools.name: process-group-terminal-kill-and-background-task-cap
tools.what: Command execution is isolated behind a terminal-backend abstraction with local, streaming, ACP-remote and PTY implementations, and its timeout semantics are about process trees rather than processes. Timeouts are absolute deadlines raced inside a `tokio::select!` so a blocked read branch cannot starve the timer (xai-grok-shell-terminal/src/streaming_local_terminal.rs:517-519, :608) - the code notes that if a read blocks, the loop stalls and the command timeout cannot fire until the next iteration. On timeout the child's whole process group is killed so grandchildren cannot hold the output pipes open (xai-grok-shell-terminal/src/local_terminal.rs:114-120), and the reaped corpse is awaited under a separate short cap (streaming_local_terminal.rs:25, :222). Background tasks are capped per session and may be waited on with an optional timeout (background_task.rs:59, :151-178). The PTY session keeps a 256 KiB output ring buffer and batches notifications every 16 ms (pty_session.rs:52-53).
invariants: Kill must target the process group, not the direct child - killing only the child leaves grandchildren holding the output pipes.
A timeout must return the synthetic result promptly rather than waiting for the killed tree to be reaped.
The timeout must be an absolute deadline selected against, because a blocking read otherwise defers it indefinitely.
The PTY output buffer is a bounded ring; it must not grow with output volume.
tools.failurePolicy: mixed - a timeout returns a synthetic result marked `timed_out: true` with signal "timeout"; an unreapable uninterruptible child is abandoned to the runtime's orphan reaper rather than hanging the call.

subagent.name: harness-only-subagent-capability-mode
subagent.what: A subagent's tool inventory is narrowed by a four-valued capability mode - ReadOnly | ReadWrite | Execute | All - applied by filtering the tool config on each tool's `ToolKind` (xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/task/types.rs:289-305). `filter_tool_config` returns immediately for `All`, otherwise retains only tools whose kind is in `allowed_tool_kinds()`, and then calls `prune_orphaned_background_task_tools`, which drops `get_task_output`/`kill_task` when no spawning tool remains so a read-only subagent is not handed lifecycle verbs for tasks it cannot create (types.rs:254-300). The mode is harness-only: it is `Option<SubagentCapabilityMode>` on the runtime overrides and is deliberately absent from the model-facing JSON schema, with tests asserting both that the schema omits `capability_mode` and that a model-supplied `capability_mode` in JSON does not round-trip (types.rs:1790-1864). The mode is set from the host side by the role that spawns the agent - for example the goal summarizer pins `SubagentCapabilityMode::ReadOnly` so the summariser can inspect but never edit or execute (xai-grok-shell/src/session/goal_summarizer.rs:140, :160).
invariants: capability_mode must never be advertised on the model-facing tool schema, and a model-authored value must be ignored - the tests exist precisely to keep this boundary.
Tools with no `kind` (MCP and custom tools built via `ToolConfig::from_id`) are preserved unconditionally, so an MCP tool is NOT narrowed by capability mode.
Pruning background-task lifecycle tools is a consequence of the filter, not a separate opt-in.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-closed on inventory (the tool config is narrowed before the subagent starts) but with an explicit fail-open carve-out for kindless MCP/custom tools.

citationCorrected.reason: the ranges ran past the end of the file; the declared loci are prune_orphaned_background_task_tools at :256 and filter_tool_config's impl at :290

subagent.name: parent-wake-safe-point-admission
subagent.what: A resident subagent can receive text from its owning parent while a turn is running, but only through the same turn-bound lifecycle as human input, and only if the sender owns an active descendant. The shell route is `SessionCommand::ParentAgentMessage`, and the message is converted into an `InputItem` carrying queue metadata of kind `parent_agent_message` so it appears in the shared queue with honest provenance (xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/parent_message.rs:99-120). The grant is `OwnedActiveDescendantGrant`, which pairs a target session id with the `ActiveAgentMessageDelivery` it authorizes, and the handle rejects any mismatch with its own target session before doing anything else (message_delivery.rs:159-161). Live steer slots are bounded by `MAX_PARENT_STEER_SLOTS = 32` so a parent's text becomes model-visible in one finite batch (parent_message.rs:45-47). The operation a parent may request is restricted to Queue or Steer - `delivery_operation` maps only those two `ActiveAgentMessageOperation` variants, and the envelope is additionally checked against `OperationSet::QUEUE_AND_STEER` (message_delivery.rs:98-103, :170-174).
invariants: The parent must own an active descendant: the grant is a distinct type carrying both target session and delivery, and there is no path that constructs it for a non-descendant.
A parent cannot use Interject or InterruptAndSend - only Queue and Steer are mapped, and the operation set check would reject the others.
The completion channel is a oneshot `PromptTurnResult` that must be settled on every path, including owner drop.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-closed - Rejected / Unsupported / ChannelClosed are returned to the caller and the message is not queued; the Drop impl settles stranded slots with an explicit error rather than leaving the parent awaiting.

subagent.name: capability-mode-meet-and-resume-identity-pin
subagent.what: A subagent's effective runtime config is resolved by first-wins precedence per field, and its capability mode is then narrowed by a meet rather than replaced. Precedence is explicit spawn-time override > role default > persona default > None meaning parent inheritance, with role and persona defaults looked up by name (xai-grok-subagent-resolution/src/overrides.rs:39-49). `intersect_capability_modes(requested, ceiling)` is the narrowing operator and its behaviour is a deliberate lattice: (None, mode) or (mode, None) yields mode; any pair containing `All` yields the other; any pair containing `ReadOnly` yields `ReadOnly`; equal ReadWrite or equal Execute yield themselves; and the incomparable pair ReadWrite/Execute collapses to `ReadOnly` (overrides.rs:22-37). Resume is gated on identity rather than on configuration: `validate_resume_identity` rejects a mismatched subagent type or an explicitly requested persona that differs from the source, while a model override is deliberately NOT validated and is silently ignored because the resumed child always inherits and pins the source model (resume.rs:1-6, :33-60).
invariants: The capability meet must stay most-restrictive-wins: the ReadWrite/Execute pair must not resolve to either input, and `All` must never win against a narrower mode.
Resume inherits the source transcript, tool state and model but re-renders the system prompt and prompt context from the current agent definition - the two halves move differently on purpose.
Model is not an identity gate on resume; a caller-supplied model override is ignored rather than rejected, so it must not be surfaced as an error.
A persona instructions-file read failure is fatal to resolution and returns early with the error populated rather than silently falling back to the parent.
subagent.failurePolicy: mixed - identity and persona-file failures are fail-closed (resolution aborts or resume is refused), while a model override on resume is fail-safe by being silently dropped in favour of the pinned source model.

subagent.name: subagent-depth-ceiling-and-unconditional-tool-stripping
subagent.what: One chokepoint shapes a child's toolset. `apply_child_tool_policy` applies the capability-mode filter, then strips the task tool and prunes orphaned background-task tools when nesting is not allowed, and ALWAYS strips workflow tools - a child can never launch a workflow at any depth (xai-grok-subagent-resolution/src/definition.rs:221). The spawn path computes `child_depth` from the parent depth and permits nesting only while the child depth is below the configured maximum (xai-grok-shell/src/agent/subagent/handle_request.rs:598-604).
invariants: Capability modes are INTERSECTED, never unioned: a request can only narrow the definition's ceiling, so a definition cannot be widened by a caller.
The workflow-tool strip is unconditional for every child at every depth - it is not a depth or capability consequence.
Depth is zero-based with a child at parent+1, so a maximum of 1 permits top-level spawns only.
The maximum depth is clamped to a minimum of 1: nesting can be adjusted but never disabled by setting zero.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-closed - an over-depth spawn loses the task tool rather than being refused outright, and an unparseable capability mode is simply absent so the definition's own ceiling applies.

subagent.name: admission-quota-with-clamped-minimum-and-workflow-bypass
subagent.what: Session-scoped spawn limiting is a small pure policy object owned by the coordinator actor: `admit(request, running)` returns Start, Enqueue or Reject, and at the limit the behaviour is queue-by-default or fail if an operator opts in (xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/task/admission.rs:6, :43-47, :102-107). Workflow-owned spawns BYPASS admission entirely, because they are governed by the workflow run's own concurrency pool instead (xai-grok-shell/src/agent/mvp_agent/subagent_spawn.rs:19).
invariants: A maximum of zero is clamped to one: a limit can be adjusted but never disabled, and the actor's queue-implies-running exit invariant needs at least one slot.
The coordinator must not re-read its configuration; the policy object's accessor is the single configured value.
The fail-path message is model-facing and explicitly tells the model not to retry.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-soft by default (queue) and fail-closed only under an operator opt-in; an unparseable behaviour value warns and keeps queueing.

subagent.name: targeted-cancellation-with-closed-admission-window
subagent.what: A single-writer coordinator actor owns the spawn queue, the pending/active/completed maps, blocking waiters, foreground deadlines, cancellation and terminal delivery, with intentionally no shared mutable state; hosts differ only in their child-runner implementation (xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/task/coordinator.rs:53). Cancellation is TARGETED rather than global - the target is a subagent id, a parent prompt id, a parent session, or a workflow run id - and a parent-session cancel additionally keeps spawn admission CLOSED until the next turn or until teardown completes, so a detached late spawn cannot outrun a stop or a session delete (xai-grok-shell/src/agent/subagent/spawn.rs:284; task/types.rs:541, :590).
invariants: One writer: no host may mutate coordinator state directly, and the child-runner seam is the only extension point.
A parent-session cancel must keep admission closed across the whole cancel window; reopening early re-admits spawns in the middle of a delete.
The teardown drain must stay authoritative over admission reopening.
Terminal status transitions must never demote an already-terminal child.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-soft with explicit backstops - a cancelled child that never finishes force-reopens admission after the drain cap with a warning rather than blocking spawns for the process lifetime, and a panicking run future is caught.

constants.name: active-message admission caps
constants.value: 8 per child, 64 total; timeouts 5 s admit, 120 s spawn-ready, 6 s finalization

subagent.name: foreground-budget-auto-backgrounding
subagent.what: A task call waits only for a bounded foreground budget. Past the deadline the child is auto-backgrounded with a log line noting it keeps running, an INTERIM result is sent carrying a backgrounded flag and success set to false so no consumer records a completed status for a live child, and the deadline is cleared so the check cannot re-fire (xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/task/coordinator_state.rs:606, :623, :639). A sibling path covers a dropped result channel: a task-owned child keeps running and leaves the outstanding set, while a workflow-owned child is cancelled.
invariants: The interim handoff must keep success FALSE: callers branch on the backgrounded flag, never on success, and reporting success would make a live child look finished.
Task-owned children survive a dropped caller while workflow-owned children do not - inverting this changes cancellation semantics for multi-agent runs.
Clearing the deadline is part of the handoff; skipping it makes the budget check fire repeatedly.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-soft - budget expiry never kills the child; the failure mode is that the model loses the synchronous result, which the auto-wake path recovers.

subagent.name: seven-input-auto-wake-suppression-gate
subagent.what: When a backgrounded child completes, whether the parent is woken is a conjunction of seven independent suppression inputs: run-in-background, not cancelled, auto-wake enabled, not block-waited, not explicitly killed, no active goal loop, and an open parent channel (xai-grok-shell/src/agent/subagent/spawn.rs:393-400). The wake decision is computed on the coordinator thread with the reservation taken there, and it stamps a surface flag so the presenter's indication matches what the injector will actually do (spawn.rs:360). The injector RE-CHECKS the goal-loop flag at inject time because it can flip in the gap (spawn.rs:429).
invariants: A CANCELLED child never wakes: the interrupt race can background a foreground child moments before its cancel lands, and waking would prompt the model immediately after the user stopped everything.
The open-channel check folds the injector's own no-channel bail into the DECISION, so a stamped wake is never promised and then not performed.
Block-waited and explicitly-killed children are suppressed to avoid double-reporting.
During an active goal loop the goal driver owns continuation, so auto-wake is suppressed.
subagent.failurePolicy: fail-closed (suppress) - every ambiguity resolves to NOT waking the model, and the completion remains visible through the ordinary between-turn reminder path instead.

safety.name: startup-applied-os-sandbox
safety.what: OS-level confinement is real and applied once, irreversibly, at process start. The crate's module doc states it provides kernel-enforced sandboxing via nono (Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS) applied once at process startup, covering in-process `tokio::fs` calls and child processes, with process-level network deliberately left open because the agent needs the LLM API while child network is blocked per-subprocess via seccomp (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:8-15). `SandboxManager::apply` resolves the profile, computes a capability set, applies it through `Sandbox::apply`, and then stores global state with an `applied` flag (lib.rs:179-262). The reverse direction is also implemented: `should_auto_allow_bash()` requires BOTH the `auto_allow_bash` setting AND `is_active()`, so sandbox state feeds the approval model rather than the other way round (lib.rs:100-106).
invariants: `apply` is documented irreversible: there is no unapply path, and the process either comes up confined or comes up under a refusal exit.
Sandbox state is process-global and set once (`OnceLock<GlobalSandboxState>`); a second apply cannot silently replace it.
`should_auto_allow_bash` must keep its `is_active()` conjunct - auto-allowing bash without an active sandbox would be an unconfined auto-approval.
safety.failurePolicy: mixed - by itself `SandboxManager::apply` degrades gracefully (an unsupported platform or a failed apply logs, records and returns Ok while leaving `applied = false`, lib.rs:196-240); the fail-closed decision is taken by the caller, which refuses to start (see the next mechanism).

constants.name: enforce feature
constants.value: on by default; without it the crate is helpers-only and nothing is kernel-enforced

safety.name: refuse-to-start-unprotected-sandbox
safety.what: The startup path is explicitly fail-closed, and it is a five-way decision rather than a boolean. `apply_sandbox` lives in the shell (it is not in the sandbox crate) and its Linux branch routes through `route_bwrap_startup`, whose variants are ReexecRequired, ReexecOptional, Verify, Refuse and Continue (xai-grok-shell/src/config/mod.rs:1458-1469). ReexecRequired execs bubblewrap and, if the exec fails, prints `Refusing to start with denied paths unprotected.` and exits 1 (mod.rs:1527-1535). Verify is the anti-spoof arm: when the process reports being inside bwrap, the required hook write-deny, read-deny and `/data` write-deny mounts are each independently re-verified, and any failure exits 1 with the message naming a `possible __GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP spoof` (mod.rs:1545-1579). Refuse covers the case where the required bwrap plan could not be prepared at all (mod.rs:1581-1587). After the Landlock/Seatbelt apply, a second independent gate refuses startup when a profile that needs protection (`is_custom || needs_hooks`) did not actually get applied (mod.rs:1591-1626).
invariants: The `__GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP` marker is never trusted on its own - `trust_bwrap_marker_for_devbox()` is hardcoded false and the Verify arm re-checks the mounts.

The set of profiles that 'require' read-deny is computed intrinsically from the profile config, not from the resolved deny set, because the resolved set is empty on error and keying on it would silently downgrade to fail-open (lib.rs:441-467).

`resolve_failure_must_refuse` composes hook-write-deny OR read-deny OR data-write-deny, so a deny-carrying custom profile extends-devbox is covered by the read-deny arm even though the hook arm does not cover it (lib.rs:497-506).
Bwrap exec failure is fatal only when requires_bwrap; otherwise it is a warning and Landlock is the fallback.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed - the process calls std::process::exit(1) rather than continuing unprotected; the only degrade path is an optional-bwrap profile, which warns and falls back to Landlock.

constants.name: refusal message
constants.value: "Refusing to start with denied paths unprotected."

safety.name: predefined-sandbox-profiles-and-anti-hollowing-merge
safety.what: Confinement is expressed as named profiles with a fixed built-in set - `workspace` (the default), `devbox`, `read-only`, `strict`, `off` - plus `Custom(name)` resolved from `~/.grok/sandbox.toml` or `.grok/sandbox.toml` (xai-grok-sandbox/src/profiles.rs:1-3, :69-112). A profile resolves to a `SandboxProfile` with read_only, read_write, deny, write_deny, default_read and restrict_network (profiles.rs:26-43), and read-deny is kernel-enforced on both platforms via the `deny` list (profiles.rs:3). The layering is deliberately not last-write-wins: the project config is additive only and is merged with `entry(name).or_insert(profile)`, so a workspace cannot redefine a profile name that already exists globally, because doing so would let a malicious workspace hollow out a user or enterprise profile while keeping the trusted name - emptying `deny` or broadening `read_write` (profiles.rs:114-167). Divergence is not silently ignored either: `sandbox_profile_conflicts` reports project profile names whose definition differs from the global one (profiles.rs:138-160). Only `read-only` and `strict` restrict child network by default (profiles.rs:80-84).
invariants: A project `.grok/sandbox.toml` can only ADD profile names; it can never replace a globally-defined profile's body.
The global config is read from `$GROK_HOME`, and the project path is workspace-relative - the two are never swapped.

`/dev/tty` may be dropped from the device set when it exists but cannot be opened (ENXIO without a controlling terminal), because a failed PathFd materialization aborts the whole Landlock ruleset - and that drop was itself the cause of a prior silent sandbox bypass under setsid/CI/headless launches (profiles.rs:183-200).
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed on policy composition (a conflicting project definition is ignored, keeping the trusted global body) and fail-soft on device enumeration (unopenable device nodes are skipped rather than aborting the ruleset); an unparsable sandbox.toml warns and is treated as absent (profiles.rs:169-181).

safety.name: bwrap-reexec-with-read-deny-placeholders
safety.what: On Linux a second, mount-level confinement layer is built as a bubblewrap re-exec. `bwrap_reexec_command_ex` composes a command that drops all capabilities (`--cap-drop ALL`), binds `/` through, mounts each deny_write path read-only, and - the interesting part - makes deny_READ paths unreadable by binding a mode-000 placeholder over them, since a read-only bind would still permit reading (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:302-369, :385-428). The placeholder is suffixed with the current PID precisely because a shared path races between concurrent grok processes and a lost race could return None, silently dropping the bind and failing open (lib.rs:394-401). If a placeholder for a deny-read path cannot be created, the function prints `refusing to start with a partial sandbox` and returns None rather than emitting a bwrap command with that deny missing (lib.rs:333-344). A containment sentinel directory is also bound in, which is what the `__GROK_INSIDE_BWRAP` verification later checks for (lib.rs:345-352).
invariants: Read-deny requires a bind-over of an unreadable placeholder; a `--ro-bind` of the real path would be useless as a read denial.
The deny-read placeholder path must be PID-suffixed - sharing it across processes reintroduces the fail-open race.
A partial plan must abort: returning a bwrap command that silently omits one deny is the failure mode this code is written to avoid.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed at plan construction (any missing placeholder or unencodable handoff returns None with an explanation, and the caller's Refuse arm exits 1); Windows/macOS compile to a None return since the path is Linux-only.

safety.name: hook-write-deny-under-sandbox
safety.what: The sandbox protects the hook installation path itself, closing the obvious escalation of writing a hook file to gain code execution on the next event. The crate exposes `requires_hook_write_deny` and the shell's startup calls `xai_grok_config::ensure_grok_hook_slots` before applying, failing the whole apply with `hook write-deny ensure failed` if the slots cannot be prepared (xai-grok-sandbox/src/lib.rs:50-64, :187-190). `SandboxManager::apply` also calls `maybe_install_namespace_lockdown_inside_bwrap` (lib.rs:191-192), and the module's own doc notes that shell fails closed when protection cannot be applied (lib.rs:50-51). `profile_enforces_hook_write_deny` and `verify_hook_write_deny_enforced` are re-exported so the startup path can both decide and then confirm the mounts took (lib.rs:39). `xai-grok-sandbox/src/hook_write_deny.rs` (415 lines) holds the plan builder, and the bwrap plan binds rootward ancestors read-write before the leaf read-only, with the ancestor ordering pinned by a test.
invariants: hook write-deny is verified after apply, not merely requested - and re-verified again in the shell's Verify arm.
The bwrap plan must RW-bind rootward ancestors before RO-binding the leaf; reversing the order would re-expose the hook directory.
A replaced leaf identity (the directory moved and recreated) must make append refuse, not silently bind the new one.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed - an ensure failure aborts apply, an unenforced verification exits 1 at startup, and a plan that cannot be built returns None so the caller refuses.

safety.name: permission-mode-projection-and-queue-drain
safety.what: The approval model is one enum projected onto one boolean. `PermissionModeKind` has Default, Ask, Auto and AlwaysApprove, and AlwaysApprove is the only variant that projects to the shell's `yolo_mode = true`, with the canonical strings default/ask/auto/always-approve as the persisted vocabulary (xai-grok-pager/src/app/actions.rs:951-979). Switching always-approve ON drains the entire pending permission queue, answering each outstanding ACP RequestPermission with AllowOnce and falling back to Cancelled - never AllowAlways - and the flag flip is deliberately ordered before the drain (xai-grok-pager/src/app/dispatch/modes.rs:284-317). Auto is gated separately by `app.auto_mode_gate`: a commit to Auto degrades to Ask when the gate is off, and a display-side downgrade clears the per-agent auto flag so no badge can read Auto while it is disabled (modes.rs:408-420, :213-232). The enabled path also routes through a managed-policy refusal (`yolo_enable_blocked` / `refuse_if_yolo_locked`) before any state mutation (modes.rs:189-204, :353-399).
invariants: AllowOnce and never AllowAlways is the drain rule: enabling bypass must not mint a durable grant for whatever happened to be pending.
The mode flag is flipped before the queue is drained - reversing that ordering would let a permission racing the drain be answered under the old mode.
A commit to Auto must be downgraded, not rejected, when auto_mode_gate is off, and the displayed badge must be downgraded too so the UI cannot disagree with the engine.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed with a soft projection - the gate either refuses the mode change outright (managed policy lock) or degrades Auto to Ask; pending requests are always answered (AllowOnce or Cancelled), so nothing is left hanging.

safety.name: hooks-as-fail-open-gates-with-deny-precedence
safety.what: Hooks act as permission gates on tool use, prompt submission and stop, with a documented fail-open posture and a strict decision precedence. `pre_tool_use` hooks can allow, ask or deny and can rewrite the tool input through `updatedInput`; prompt and stop gates can block; and the crate doc states the posture directly - fail-open by default, a hook error never blocks (xai-grok-hooks/src/lib.rs:11-17). The precedence is implemented as a match over accumulated per-hook outcomes and is total: a GateBlock yields Deny, otherwise a pending ask yields Ask, otherwise a deferring hook yields Defer, otherwise Allow (xai-grok-hooks/src/dispatcher.rs:316-326). The fail-open rule is called out as a security comment at the sequential gate: a hook that errors contributes nothing, and only a healthy deny blocks (dispatcher.rs:77). Distinct gate kinds get distinct timeouts rather than one global value: `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECS = 5` for observe and tool gates, `DEFAULT_VERIFICATION_GATE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 600` for stop and post-tool gates because they run builds and linters, and `DEFAULT_PROMPT_GATE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 30` because a prompt gate runs before every prompt and a stuck hook would stall the session (xai-grok-hooks/src/config.rs:122-135, :168-178). Session-end hooks get their own bounded budget with a hard ceiling: default 1500 ms, maximum 60000 ms, and an out-of-range env value warns and falls back rather than applying (config.rs:137-166). A `timeout: 0` in a hook's config floors to the event default rather than disabling the bound (config.rs:608-609).
invariants: Fail-open is the stated default and is enforced by the sequential gate discarding errored hook results; a change that made a crashing hook block would invert the documented posture.
Precedence is Deny > Ask > Defer > Allow and is expressed as one exhaustive match, so no ordering of hook registration can promote an allow over an ask.
Timeout zero means 'use the event default', never 'no bound'.
The session-end budget has a hard maximum; the env var can raise the default up to the ceiling but not past it.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-open on hook faults (an erroring or timing-out hook contributes nothing) but fail-closed on hook decisions (a healthy deny with exit code 2 blocks regardless of JSON); the combination means only a positive, successful deny stops a call.

safety.name: retention-and-secret-redaction
safety.what: Secret redaction is a code capability applied before values leave the process. `xai-grok-secrets` exposes a sanitizer surface rather than a policy: `redact_json_string_values`, `redact_secrets`, `redact_url`, `redact_user_paths` and a `walk_json_strings` traversal used to apply redaction across a JSON document (xai-grok-secrets/src/lib.rs:1-6). URL and user-path redaction are separate functions, so a URL that embeds a credential and a path that embeds a username are handled by different rules. The crate is classified as `safety` by the module checklist's keyword hint; from the code it is a data-handling capability that happens to sit in the credentials family.
invariants: Redaction walks string values rather than whole documents, so a structured value cannot be missed because it sits inside a nested object.
URL and path redaction are distinct entry points - collapsing them would either over-redact paths or under-redact URLs with embedded credentials.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-soft - redaction is a pure transformation with no I/O and no error path (the exported functions return the redacted value), so its guarantee depends entirely on call-site coverage.

safety.name: root-owned-managed-policy-pin
safety.what: Deployment policy enters as a separate, higher-authority config layer rather than as a setting the user can flip back. Requirements load from unordered-on-disk but strictly-ordered layers: the user-writable `$GROK_HOME/requirements.toml` first, then the root-owned system file from `system_config_dir()`, then the macOS MDM managed-preferences layer last so it wins the deep merge - and the MDM layer is marked `is_system` exactly like the root-owned file (xai-grok-config/src/validation.rs:63-95). `is_system` is a stored flag rather than a re-derivation, with the stated reason that the source path is `GROK_HOME`-influenced and could carry `..` (validation.rs:56-58). `load_merged_requirements` deep-merges user then system so a user pin cannot win a conflict (validation.rs:97-106). The concrete user-facing effect is the always-approve lock: `[ui] disable_bypass_permissions_mode = true` in a requirements layer pins bypass off, with `[ui] yolo = false` kept as a back-compat alias, and the refusal string names the policy explicitly (xai-grok-workspace/src/permission/resolution.rs:918-932, :952, :1004).
invariants: Order is user -> root-owned system -> MDM, and later layers win; nothing may be inserted after the MDM layer.
Security decisions must read the stored `is_system` boolean, never re-derive it from the path.

The `fail_closed` key is stripped during normalization so it cannot deep-merge into the effective config and leak into a user config write; a regression test exists for exactly that (xai-grok-shell/tests/test_config_update_isolation.rs).
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed - `fail_closed = true` in a requirements layer turns an invalid `[[version_overrides]]` for this build into a startup error (RequirementsError::InvalidVersionOverrides) rather than a skipped layer, and an unreadable requirements.toml is treated as fail_closed armed (xai-grok-config/src/managed_cache.rs:180-194).

safety.name: macos-mdm-forced-managed-preferences
safety.what: On macOS an additional admin layer arrives through OS managed preferences rather than a file, and it is deliberately strong: `RequirementsSource::Mdm` is a distinct variant with no path at all, precisely so a caller cannot call `exists()` on it or read it as a file, and its label is the synthetic source id `ai.x.grok:...` (xai-grok-config/src/validation.rs:32-49). The layer is normalized through the same path as every other source and pushed last, and it is marked `is_system` so security decisions trust it like the root-owned layer (validation.rs:84-93). `managed_requirements_from` gates the whole thing on the forced read returning Some: a read that fails, or a value that is not valid base64, yields None - the layer is absent rather than partially applied (xai-grok-config/src/macos_managed.rs:22-29, :167-173). MDM is also a source for the sandbox-mode allow list, read through CoreFoundation and deliberately not environment-expanded.
invariants: The MDM layer has no filesystem path by construction; code that wants to inspect it must match on the enum, not build a PathBuf.
MDM is pushed after the root-owned system file so it wins the merge; the doc comment states this as the reason for its position.
A failed or unparsable forced read must produce no layer at all, not a partially-decoded one.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed in effect - a broken MDM read removes the admin layer rather than installing a wrong one, but because the layer is admin-forced this also means policy is absent; the read itself is gated on an explicit `Some`.

safety.name: ed25519-signed-policy-at-rest-fail-closed-arm
safety.what: The cloud-cached requirements file is signed at rest once a key is embedded, and the managed cache carries an explicit armed state. `signed_policy.rs` treats a signed-ABSENT slot as requiring the file to be empty on disk, with the stated reason that a locally planted `requirements.toml` - the highest-precedence layer - is tamper and not noise (xai-grok-config/src/signed_policy.rs:375-389). The cache exposes `fail_closed_policy_armed_at`, which returns true when the sync marker records `fail_closed`, OR the on-disk requirements.toml parses as fail_closed, OR the file exists but is unreadable (managed_cache.rs:180-194). The unreadable case logs `requirements.toml unreadable; treating as fail_closed armed` and takes the armed branch.
invariants: A signed-absent slot must be empty on disk; non-empty content there is tamper, not a normal unverifiable state.
Unreadable is treated the same as fail_closed-armed - the failure mode of a permission error must not be 'policy off'.
There are three independent ways to be armed (marker, parsed flag, unreadable file); removing any one narrows the arming surface.
safety.failurePolicy: fail-closed - an unreadable or tampered policy file arms fail-closed rather than disabling policy.

safety.name: requirement-pinned-feature-flags-with-seven-tier-ladder
